presentingComplaint: High-grade fever with rigors for 5 days, now drowsy with reduced urine output and cold peripheries.
history: Migrant construction worker who returned 12 days ago from a 3-month posting in a forested district of Chhattisgarh (high-transmission zone). Five days of paroxysmal fever with shaking chills and drenching sweats, initially alternate-day then daily, with severe myalgia and headache. Over the past 24 hours he became progressively confused, passed only a small volume of dark 'tea-coloured' urine, and developed breathlessness. No cough, dysuria, diarrhoea, or rash. Took no chemoprophylaxis. No prior antibiotics or hospitalisation. No comorbidities; not immunocompromised.
examination: Ill, drowsy and toxic-looking (GCS 13, E3V4M6). Deeply icteric. Peripheries cold and mottled with capillary refill 4 s. Mild pallor. Tender splenomegaly 3 cm below costal margin and smooth hepatomegaly. Chest with bibasal crepitations; no focal consolidation. No neck stiffness, no rash, no eschar. Passing scanty dark urine via catheter.

labs.parasiteIndex: P. falciparum ring-form parasitaemia 6.2% + P. vivax trophozoites/gametocytes co-present

imaging: Chest radiograph: bilateral lower-zone interstitial opacities consistent with early ARDS/pulmonary oedema; no lobar consolidation. USG abdomen: hepatosplenomegaly, no biliary obstruction, no abscess.
microbiology: Thick and thin peripheral smear (Giemsa): P. falciparum asexual ring forms with high parasitaemia PLUS P. vivax trophozoites and gametocytes — mixed infection confirmed. Rapid diagnostic test positive for both HRP-2 (falciparum) and pan-Plasmodium/vivax LDH. Two sets of blood cultures drawn before antibiotics: no growth at 48 h. Urine culture negative. Dengue NS1/IgM negative; leptospira IgM negative; scrub typhus IgM negative.
differentialDiagnoses: Severe mixed-species malaria with septic shock and multi-organ dysfunction (target)
Bacterial sepsis / Gram-negative bacteraemia (co-infection must be excluded and empirically covered)
finalDiagnosis: Severe mixed malaria (P. falciparum + P. vivax) complicated by septic shock, acute kidney injury, hyperbilirubinaemia, metabolic acidosis with hyperlactataemia, thrombocytopenia and hypoglycaemia.
citations: WHO Guidelines for Malaria — Severe Malaria Management 2023
NVBDCP/NCVBDC India National Drug Policy on Malaria 2013 (rev.)
Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Malaria
stewardship: This is severe malaria: definitive therapy is IV artesunate 2.4 mg/kg at 0, 12 and 24 h then daily, transitioning to a full oral ACT (artemether-lumefantrine) once tolerating orally, plus a 14-day radical-cure course of primaquine after G6PD testing to clear the P. vivax hypnozoites. Because severe malaria with shock is clinically indistinguishable from, and frequently co-exists with, invasive bacterial infection (esp. non-typhoidal Salmonella / Gram-negative bacteraemia), WHO advises empiric broad-spectrum antibacterial cover after taking blood cultures — IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily here. Stewardship endpoint: with two negative blood cultures at 48 h, no localising bacterial source, and clear clinical + parasitological response to artesunate, de-escalate by STOPPING ceftriaxone at 48 h and continuing antimalarial therapy alone. Antimalarials are not de-escalated.
contraindications: Avoid primaquine until G6PD status known (haemolysis risk) and defer in pregnancy
Do not use oral-only ACT as sole initial therapy in severe malaria — parenteral artesunate is mandatory
Avoid nephrotoxic and QT-prolonging agents; monitor for delayed post-artesunate haemolysis
Renal-dose all cleared drugs given AKI (creatinine 3.1)
edgeCases: Mixed infection: falciparum drives the severe/shock phenotype while vivax mandates hypnozoite eradication — treating only falciparum leads to later relapse
Persisting shock/lactate despite adequate antimalarials should trigger active search for occult bacterial co-infection rather than reflex antibiotic continuation
Hypoglycaemia may be both a malaria complication and an artesunate/quinine effect — recheck glucose frequently
expectedMaiK: Severe malaria (WHO criteria: impaired consciousness, shock, AKI, jaundice, hyperlactataemia, hyperparasitaemia) on a positive mixed-species smear from an endemic-area returnee mandates immediate IV artesunate; empiric antibiotics cover concurrent bacterial sepsis and are de-escalated once cultures are negative.

regressionAssertions: Engine must return MIXED_MALARIA as the primary diagnosis given a confirmed mixed P. falciparum + P. vivax smear.
IV artesunate must be recommended as definitive therapy for this severe malaria presentation.
Empiric ceftriaxone must be de-escalated/stopped at 48h given negative blood cultures and no bacterial source.
Primaquine radical cure must be flagged as G6PD-dependent for vivax hypnozoite clearance.
Malaria smear findings must NOT be overridden by a purely bacterial-sepsis diagnosis.
